docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
feu (French word for "fire" 🔥) is a lightweight Python library designed to help manage Python packages and their versions across different Python environments. It provides utilities to:

  • Check package availability: Verify if packages and modules are available in your environment
  • Install packages intelligently: Install packages with version compatibility checks for your target environment
  • Version management: Find the closest valid package version for your target environment
  • Package configuration: Maintain a registry of known package version compatibility, and discover it automatically from PyPI when it isn't already registered
  • Version utilities: Compare, filter and sort versions, fetch the versions published on PyPI, and read dependency bounds from pyproject.toml
  • Git and GitHub utilities: Get the tags of a local git repository, and fetch and sort repository metadata from the GitHub API

The library is particularly useful for projects that need to support multiple Python versions, free-threaded builds, OSes, and CPU architectures, and want to ensure they install compatible package versions.

docs.title: Key Features
docs.text:
• Target-aware: Automatically selects compatible package versions based on the Python version, free-threadedness, OS, and CPU architecture
  • CLI interface: Command-line tools for package management tasks
  • Lightweight: Minimal dependencies (only packaging required for core functionality)
  • Extensible: Registry of common packages (numpy, pandas, polars, torch, etc.) with known version constraints, plus PyPI-backed discovery for anything not in the registry

docs.title: Quick Example
docs.text:
>>> from feu import is_package_available
>>> from feu.compat import Target, find_closest_version
>>> is_package_available("packaging")
True
>>> target = Target(python_version="3.9", os="linux", arch="x86_64")
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "2.3.0", target)
'2.0.2'
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "1.*", target)
'1.26.4'

docs.title: API stability
docs.text: While feu is in development stage, no API is guaranteed to be stable from one release to the next. In fact, it is very likely that the API will change multiple times before a stable 1.0.0 release. In practice, this means that upgrading feu to a new version will possibly break any code that was using the old version of feu.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
feu provides a command-line interface (CLI) for package management tasks. To use the CLI, you need to install the optional cli dependency:

pip install 'feu[cli]'

docs.title: Exit Status
docs.text:
The standard output holds only the answer of a command, the logs and the error messages go to the standard error (--verbose logs the executed commands), and the exit status carries the result:

  • 0: success, or a valid version;
  • 1: a negative answer (no compatible version, or check-valid-version printed False);
  • 2: a usage error (unknown option, missing option, invalid version request).

feu --version prints the version. feu is a console script; python -m feu is equivalent.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: The reference below is generated from the code (mkdocs-click), so it cannot drift. install installs into the interpreter that runs feu for the current target, so it has no target option. The platform (OS and CPU architecture) is always the current one: there is no --os or --arch option.

docs.title: feu
docs.text:
Implement the main entrypoint, which groups the commands.

Usage:

feu [OPTIONS] COMMAND [ARGS]...

Options:

  --version  Show the version and exit.
  --verbose  Log the executed commands on the standard error.
  --help     Show this message and exit.

docs.title: check-valid-version
docs.text:
Print if a package version is valid for a target.

True is printed and the exit status is 0 if the version is valid or if the package is not configured for the target. Otherwise False is printed and the exit status is 1.

Args: pkg_name: The package name. pkg_version: The package version request to check. python_version: The python version. If not provided, the current python version is used. free_threaded: Whether the target is a free-threaded build. If not provided, the current interpreter's free-threaded status is used.

Example: 

$ feu check-valid-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2 --python-version=3.10

Usage:

feu check-valid-version [OPTIONS]

Options:

  -n, --pkg-name TEXT             Package name  [required]
  -v, --pkg-version TEXT          Package version request: an exact version
                                  e.g. '2.0.2', a wildcard e.g. '2.*' or an
                                  empty string for the latest version.
                                  [default: ""]
  -p, --python-version TEXT       Python version e.g. '3.12' or '3.14t'.
                                  Default: the current Python version.
  -f, --free-threaded / --no-free-threaded
                                  Whether the target is a free-threaded build.
                                  Default: the current interpreter.
  --help                          Show this message and exit.

docs.title: find-closest-version
docs.text:
Print the closest valid version of a package for a target.

The standard output holds only the version to install. For a wildcard or an empty version request that lies in an open-ended range, the request itself is printed. If no version is compatible with the target, the message is printed on the standard error, the standard output is empty and the exit status is 1.

Args: pkg_name: The package name. pkg_version: The package version request to check. python_version: The python version. If not provided, the current python version is used. free_threaded: Whether the target is a free-threaded build. If not provided, the current interpreter's free-threaded status is used.

Example: 

$ feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2 --python-version=3.10

Usage:

feu find-closest-version [OPTIONS]

Options:

  -n, --pkg-name TEXT             Package name  [required]
  -v, --pkg-version TEXT          Package version request: an exact version
                                  e.g. '2.0.2', a wildcard e.g. '2.*' or an
                                  empty string for the latest version.
                                  [default: ""]
  -p, --python-version TEXT       Python version e.g. '3.12' or '3.14t'.
                                  Default: the current Python version.
  -f, --free-threaded / --no-free-threaded
                                  Whether the target is a free-threaded build.
                                  Default: the current interpreter.
  --help                          Show this message and exit.

docs.title: install
docs.text:
Install a package and associated packages.

The package is installed in the interpreter that runs feu, for the current target. The closest compatible version is installed if pkg_version is not compatible. The exit status is 1 if no version is compatible and 2 if an argument is invalid (e.g. a malformed wildcard).

Args: pkg_name: The package name e.g. 'pandas'. pkg_version: The version request of the package to install: an exact version, a wildcard (e.g. '2.*') or an empty string for the latest version. pkg_extras: Optional package extra dependencies, separated by commas e.g. 'dev,doc'. An empty string means no extra. installer_name: The package installer name to use to install the packages. installer_args: Optional arguments to pass to the package installer, as a single string e.g. '--upgrade'. It is split once with shlex.split. The valid arguments depend on the package installer.

Example: 

$ feu install --installer-name=pip --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2

Usage:

feu install [OPTIONS]

Options:

  -n, --pkg-name TEXT        Package name  [required]
  -v, --pkg-version TEXT     Package version request: an exact version e.g.
                             '2.0.2', a wildcard e.g. '2.*' or an empty string
                             for the latest version.  [default: ""]
  -e, --pkg-extras TEXT      Package extra dependencies, separated by commas
                             e.g. 'dev,doc'.  [default: ""]
  -i, --installer-name TEXT  The package installer.  [default: pip]
  -a, --installer-args TEXT  Arguments to pass to the package installer, split
                             once like a shell would.  [default: ""]
  --help                     Show this message and exit.

docs.title: package-versions
docs.text:
Write the versions to test of the dependencies of a project.

The dependencies are read from [project.dependencies] and [project.optional-dependencies]. The output is a JSON object that maps each package to the latest version of each minor (or major) version at or above its lower bound.

Args: pyproject: The pyproject.toml file. output: The JSON file to write, or None for the standard output. major_only: The packages for which only the major versions are kept.

Example: 

$ feu package-versions --pyproject pyproject.toml --output dev/config/package_versions.json

Usage:

feu package-versions [OPTIONS]

Options:

  --pyproject FILE   The pyproject.toml file to read the dependencies from.
                     [default: pyproject.toml]
  --output FILE      The JSON file to write. Default: the standard output.
  --major-only TEXT  A package for which only the latest version of each major
                     version is kept. Repeat the option for several packages.
                     [default: packaging]
  --help             Show this message and exit.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
Find the closest valid NumPy version for Python 3.10 and for an older NumPy on Python 3.11:

$ feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2 --python-version=3.10
2.0.2
$ feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=1.0.0 --python-version=3.11
1.23.2

A wildcard or an empty version request is resolved like a version. The request itself is printed when the latest compatible release is in an open-ended range, so that the installer picks the real latest release:

$ feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version='1.*' --python-version=3.9
1.26.4
$ feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version='1.24.*' --python-version=3.14
No version of package numpy matches '1.24.*' for target Target(python_version='3.14', ...)
$ echo $?
1

Check if a version is valid. The exit status is 0 when the version is valid:

$ feu check-valid-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2 --python-version=3.10
True
$ feu check-valid-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=1.0.0 --python-version=3.11
False

Install a package, with extras and installer arguments:

feu install --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2
feu install --pkg-name=pandas --pkg-version='2.*' --pkg-extras=performance
feu install --installer-name=uv --installer-args='--upgrade' --pkg-name=numpy

Write the versions to test of the dependencies of a project (it replaces the dev/generate_versions.py script that is copied in several repositories):

feu package-versions --pyproject pyproject.toml --output dev/config/package_versions.json

docs.title: Use in a shell script or a workflow
docs.text:
The standard output holds only the answer, so it can be captured. An unsupported request makes the step fail instead of installing pkg==None:

VERSION=$(feu find-closest-version --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version=2.0.2 --python-version=3.10) \
  && feu install --pkg-name=numpy --pkg-version="$VERSION"

docs.title: Get Started
docs.text: It is highly recommended to install in a virtual environment to keep your system in order.

docs.title: Installing with pip (recommended)
docs.text:
The following command installs the latest version of the library:

pip install feu

To make the package as slim as possible, only the packages required to use feu are installed. It is possible to install all the optional dependencies by running the following command:

pip install 'feu[all]'

It is also possible to install specific optional dependencies:

  • feu[cli] - Install CLI support (click)
  • feu[git] - Install git support (gitpython)
  • feu[requests] - Install HTTP request support (requests, urllib3)
  • feu[rich] - Install rich console/formatting support (rich)

For example:

pip install 'feu[cli,git]'

docs.title: Installing from source
docs.text:
To install feu from source, you can follow the steps below. First, you will need to install uv. uv is a fast Python package installer and resolver used to manage dependencies in this project.

You can install uv using:

# On macOS and Linux
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh

# Or with pip
pip install uv

Then, clone the git repository:

git clone git@github.com:durandtibo/feu.git
cd feu

It is recommended to create a Python 3.11+ virtual environment. The easiest way is to use the provided Makefile command:

make setup-venv

This command automatically:

  1. Updates uv to the latest version
  2. Creates a Python 3.14 virtual environment
  3. Installs invoke task runner
  4. Installs all dependencies including development and documentation dependencies

Alternatively, you can manually set up the environment:

# Create a virtual environment with uv
uv venv --python 3.14

# Activate the virtual environment
source .venv/bin/activate

# Install the package with all dependencies
uv sync --all-extras --group dev --group docs

After installation, you can verify everything is working by running the tests:

inv test.unit --cov

docs.title: Migration to 0.9
docs.text: feu 0.9 is a breaking release (feu is 0.x). The names that other repositories depend on are kept: from feu import compare_version, feu.imports.is_package_available, the feu.testing marks, feu.local_git.get_last_version_tag_name, and the short and long names of the CLI options -n, -v, -e, -i, -a, -p.

docs.title: Behaviour changes
docs.text:
• A target without os and arch is no longer a no-op. find_closest_version("numpy", "2.3.0", Target("3.9")) returned "2.3.0"; it now returns "2.0.2" (the union of the platforms). install_package_closest_version uses the full current target, and the examples of the README return what they document.
  • A version is a request. "", None and a wildcard ("2.*") are accepted wherever a version is, checked against the registry and resolved. A wildcard is no longer skipped by the compatibility check; a wildcard with no match raises UnsupportedVersionError.
  • Package names are canonical (PEP 503) in the registries, the resolver registry, the pyproject reader and the PyPI functions. The sklearn resolver key is gone.
  • find-closest-version prints only the version; an unsupported request exits 1 with the message on standard error (it printed None and exited 0). check-valid-version exits 1 when the version is not valid. An invalid argument exits 2.
  • pip installs into the interpreter that runs feu (sys.executable -m pip), and a missing pip or uv raises RuntimeError before any command.
  • Wheels: macosx_*_universal2 wheels and compressed tag sets count for every platform they support. The shipped data changed for 10 macOS targets.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
These are the rules feu follows. Each one is enforced in one place, not by the discipline of each function, and says how you can rely on it.

# Property What you can rely on 1 Lightweight The only required dependency is packaging. import feu, import feu.compat and import feu.install import no optional library, read no file other than code, and do no network call. 2 Explicit optional dependencies A feature that needs click, gitpython, requests or rich checks it first. A missing package raises MissingPackageError (a ModuleNotFoundError and a RuntimeError) whose message gives the pip and uv pip command. 3 Target-aware A compatibility answer is a function of (package, version, Target). Code that acts on the current environment uses the full current target (resolve_target()). 4 No silent no-op Every field of the target is used or the call fails. A field left to None means "any platform". An unknown package is permissive and can be detected with registry.has_package. 5 Data-driven and reproducible The built-in constraints are generated from the wheels published on PyPI by one command (dev/generate_compat_data.py), sorted and dated. No constraint is written by hand. 6 Extensible by registration A package constraint, an installer or a dependency resolver is added by registering one value in a registry instance. No subclassing is needed to add data, and no registry is process-global class state. 7 Standards compliant Package names are canonicalised once (PEP 503), versions are packaging versions (PEP 440), requirements are packaging requirements (PEP 508) and wheel names are parsed by packaging. 8 No shell, no string-built command An external command is an argument vector. pip runs as sys.executable -m pip, so it installs into the interpreter that runs feu. The command is logged before it runs. 9 Fresh and immutable Availability checks are cached and clear_availability_caches() resets them (install_package calls it after a success). The PyPI and GitHub values that are cached are immutable, so no caller can corrupt a cache. 10 Deterministic order Versions are ordered by PEP 440, never as strings. A mapping that is returned or written is sorted. The generated data has a date and no timestamp. 11 A thin CLI The CLI is the same API behind click. Standard output holds only the answer (it is used in $(...)), logs go to standard error, the exit status carries the result (0 ok, 1 negative answer, 2 usage error). 12 Strict, typed, documented Options are keyword-only. Invalid input raises ValueError or TypeError with an explicit message. Every public function has a doctest, and the examples of this guide are doctests too. 13 Layered The imports go one way: imports, utils, version, compat, install, cli. imports imports nothing from feu. A test checks it. 14 Cross-platform, Python 3.11 and newer Linux, macOS and Windows behave the same: there is no shlex rule that depends on os.name and no PATH lookup of pip. 15 A version is a request Wherever a function takes the version of a package to install or to validate, it accepts an exact version (2.4.0), a wildcard (2.4.*) or an empty string / None (the latest). A request with no compatible version raises UnsupportedVersionError, never crashes.

docs.title: A few of them, as examples
docs.text:
The target is used entirely (property 4), and the answer for a target without a platform is the union over the platforms:

>>> from feu.compat import Target, find_closest_version
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "99.0.0", Target("3.9"))
'2.0.2'

Package names are canonical (property 7), so the spelling does not matter:

>>> from feu.compat import get_default_compat_registry
>>> registry = get_default_compat_registry()
>>> registry.has_package("Scikit_Learn")
True

A version request is parsed by one parser (property 15):

>>> from feu.version import parse_version_request
>>> [str(parse_version_request(text)) for text in (None, "", "2.4.0", "2.*")]
['', '', '2.4.0', '2.*']

The orders are PEP 440 orders (property 10):

>>> from feu.version import sort_versions
>>> sort_versions(["1.10.0", "1.9.0", "1.2.0"])
['1.2.0', '1.9.0', '1.10.0']

An external command is an argument vector built from the interpreter (property 8):

>>> import sys
>>> from feu.install import PipInstaller
>>> PipInstaller.prefix == (sys.executable, "-m", "pip", "install")
True

docs.title: Usage Guide
docs.text: This guide shows the main features of feu. The examples are doctests: they are run by the test suite (tests/unit/test_docs.py), so they cannot drift from the code. The examples that need the network are marked as skipped. The rules the package follows are in Properties.

docs.title: Checking Package Availability
docs.text:
is_package_available looks a package up without importing it, is_module_available imports the module. The checks are cached, so call clear_availability_caches() if you change sys.path or sys.modules yourself. install_package clears the caches after a successful installation.

>>> from feu import is_module_available, is_package_available
>>> is_package_available("packaging")
True
>>> is_package_available("not_an_installed_package")
False
>>> is_module_available("packaging.version")
True

A module that is installed but broken (for example a missing shared library) is reported as not available by is_module_available, and a warning is logged.

The optional libraries of feu (click, gitpython, requests, rich) are imported lazily: import feu imports none of them. A feature that needs one of them raises feu.imports.MissingPackageError, which is a ModuleNotFoundError and a RuntimeError. The message gives the pip install and uv pip install commands:

>>> from feu.imports import MissingPackageError, check_package
>>> try:
...     check_package("not_an_installed_package")
... except MissingPackageError as error:
...     print(error.name)
not_an_installed_package

docs.title: Version Comparison and Requests
docs.text:
compare_version compares the installed version of a package to a version. It returns False if the package is not installed:

>>> import operator
>>> from feu import compare_version
>>> compare_version("packaging", operator.ge, "20.0")
True
>>> compare_version("not_an_installed_package", operator.ge, "1.0")
False

Wherever a function takes the version of a package to install or to validate, it accepts a version request: an exact version ("2.4.0"), a wildcard ("2.4.*", "2.*") or an empty string / None for the latest version. A wildcard is digits and dots followed by one trailing .*; anything else with a * raises ValueError:

>>> from feu.version import parse_version_request
>>> parse_version_request("2.4.*")
VersionRequest(text='2.4.*', exact=None, prefix=(2, 4))
>>> parse_version_request("").is_latest
True
>>> parse_version_request("2.*.1")
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
ValueError: invalid version wildcard '2.*.1': a wildcard is digits and dots followed by one trailing '.*', e.g. '2.4.*'

docs.title: Finding Compatible Versions
docs.text:
A Target is the environment a constraint applies to: the Python version, the free-threaded flag, the operating system and the CPU architecture. os and arch left to None mean "any platform" when a target is used for a lookup: the answer is then the union of the versions published for at least one platform. resolve_target() is the current environment (the platform is always the current one).

>>> from feu.compat import Target, find_closest_version, is_valid_version
>>> target = Target(python_version="3.9", os="linux", arch="x86_64")
>>> is_valid_version("numpy", "2.0.2", target)
True
>>> is_valid_version("numpy", "2.3.0", target)
False
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "99.0.0", target)
'2.0.2'

The shipped data holds the compatible ranges, not a list of releases. A wildcard (1.*) is matched against the releases that are downloaded from PyPI when it is resolved, so it never goes stale and no new feu release is needed when a package publishes a version. The exact version and the latest version ("") need no download: the latest version is the request itself when the last range is open-ended (the newest release was compatible when the data was generated), so that the installer picks the real latest release, and the highest upper bound otherwise. A wildcard resolves to the request itself in the same case. There is no offline fallback: resolving a wildcard without network access raises the error of the download.

>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "1.*", target)  # doctest: +SKIP
'1.26.4'
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "", target)
'2.0.2'
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "1.24.*", Target("3.14", os="linux", arch="x86_64"))  # doctest: +SKIP
Traceback (most recent call last):
    ...
feu.compat.registry.UnsupportedVersionError: No version of package numpy matches '1.24.*' for target Target(python_version='3.14', free_threaded=False, os='linux', arch='x86_64')

A package without data accepts any version, which has_package lets you detect. If the package is configured but no version supports the target, is_valid_version returns False and find_closest_version raises feu.compat.UnsupportedVersionError.

>>> from feu.compat import get_default_compat_registry, get_compatible_versions
>>> registry = get_default_compat_registry()
>>> registry.has_package("numpy"), registry.has_package("not-a-package")
(True, False)
>>> get_compatible_versions("numpy", target, "1.26.*")  # doctest: +SKIP
['1.26.0', '1.26.1', '1.26.2', '1.26.3', '1.26.4']

The built-in data is one JSON file per package in feu/compat/data. It is parsed the first time a package is looked up, and registry.packages() lists the packages without parsing any file.

docs.title: Your Own Constraints
docs.text:
Register a constraint and, if you do not want them downloaded, the versions you know in a registry instance (CompatRegistry(version_source=...) takes your own function to list the versions). Every function takes an optional registry=; register_compat adds to the default registry. A registration into a shipped package first loads it, so the conflict check sees the shipped entries (use exist_ok=True to overwrite).

>>> from feu.compat import CompatRegistry, VersionRange, get_compatible_versions
>>> target = Target(python_version="3.11")
>>> registry = CompatRegistry()
>>> registry.register("my_package", target, ranges=[VersionRange("1.2.0", "2.0.0")])
>>> registry.register_versions("my_package", ["1.2.0", "1.5.0", "2.0.0", "3.0.0"])
>>> find_closest_version("my_package", "3.0.0", target, registry=registry)
'2.0.0'
>>> get_compatible_versions("my_package", target, "1.*", registry=registry)
['1.2.0', '1.5.0']

docs.title: Installing Packages
docs.text:
install_package installs as written. install_package_closest_version first resolves the version request for the current target (or target=), and raises UnsupportedVersionError before running any command if no compatible version matches.

from feu import install_package, install_package_closest_version
from feu.install import InstallerSpec
from feu.utils.package import PackageSpec

install_package(
    installer=InstallerSpec(name="pip"),
    package=PackageSpec(name="numpy", version="2.0.2"),
)
install_package_closest_version(
    installer=InstallerSpec(name="uv", arguments="--upgrade"),
    package=PackageSpec(name="numpy", version="2.*"),
)

An installer builds one command, as an argument vector (never a shell string), and the packages are installed in the interpreter that runs feu: pip runs as <sys.executable> -m pip install ... and uv as uv pip install --python <sys.executable> .... A RuntimeError is raised before any command if pip is not available in that interpreter (for example in an environment created by uv venv) or if uv is not on the PATH.

>>> from packaging.requirements import Requirement
>>> from feu.install import InstallerSpec, PipInstaller
>>> command = PipInstaller("-U --pre").command([Requirement("numpy==2.0.2")])
>>> command[1:]
['-m', 'pip', 'install', '-U', '--pre', 'numpy==2.0.2']
>>> InstallerSpec("pip", arguments="-U --pre").arguments
('-U', '--pre')

The arguments of an installer are a string, split once with shlex.split, or a list of strings, which is used as is. pipx is not a built-in installer: it installs an application into an isolated environment, not into the current environment.

docs.title: Dependency resolvers
docs.text:
Some packages need an extra requirement: pandas before 2.2.2 needs numpy<2.0.0. A resolver is a function from a PackageSpec to a list of packaging.requirements.Requirement. The resolver reasons on the whole version request:

>>> from feu.install.resolver import resolve
>>> from feu.utils.package import PackageSpec
>>> resolve(PackageSpec("pandas", "2.1.1"))
[<Requirement('pandas==2.1.1')>, <Requirement('numpy<2.0.0')>]
>>> resolve(PackageSpec("pandas", "2.1.*"))
[<Requirement('pandas==2.1.*')>, <Requirement('numpy<2.0.0')>]
>>> resolve(PackageSpec("pandas", "2.*"))
[<Requirement('pandas==2.*')>]

Register your own installer or resolver in the default registries with register_installer(name, installer_class) and register_resolver(package, resolver). See the architecture page.

docs.title: Discovering Compatibility from PyPI
docs.text:
feu can query PyPI to discover which package versions are compatible with each target. The result is the data that dev/generate_compat_data.py writes to feu/compat/data:

from feu.compat import discover_compat_targets, show_compat_targets

# The considered versions and the ranges of each target, from the wheels on PyPI.
discovery = discover_compat_targets("numpy")

# Pretty-print the matrix as a table (requires the `rich` extra)
show_compat_targets(discovery, pkg_name="numpy")

docs.title: Working with Git Repositories
docs.text:
If you have installed the git extra (pip install 'feu[git]'):

from feu.local_git import get_last_tag_name, get_last_version_tag_name, get_tags

tags = get_tags()  # sorted by commit date
last_tag = get_last_tag_name()
last_version_tag = get_last_version_tag_name()  # e.g. "v1.2.3"

# By default, a RuntimeError is raised if no tag is found.
last_tag = get_last_tag_name(raise_error=False)  # None instead

If you have installed the requests extra (pip install 'feu[requests]'):

from feu.github import fetch_github_metadata, fetch_github_repos, sort_repos_by_key

# The `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable, if set, increases the rate limit.
metadata = fetch_github_metadata(owner="durandtibo", repo="feu")  # a read-only mapping
repos = fetch_github_repos(owner="durandtibo")  # a tuple of read-only mappings
by_stars = sort_repos_by_key(repos, key="stargazers_count", reverse=True)

docs.title: Testing Utilities
docs.text:
feu.testing provides pytest marks to skip a test when an optional dependency is (not) available:

from feu.testing import click_available, requests_not_available


@click_available
def test_cli_feature(): ...


@requests_not_available
def test_error_without_requests(): ...

Each mark has an ..._available variant (skips the test if the dependency is not available) and an ..._not_available variant (skips the test if the dependency is available). Marks are provided for click, git, jax, matplotlib, numpy, pandas, pip, polars, pyarrow, requests, rich, scipy, sklearn, torch, uv, and xarray.

>>> for python_version in ("3.9", "3.10"):
...     target = Target(python_version, os="linux", arch="x86_64")

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
The imports go one way (property 13). A module imports only the layers on its left; imports imports nothing from feu. tests/unit/test_layers.py checks it.

imports  ->  utils  ->  version  ->  compat  ->  install  ->  cli
Layer What it does I/O imports Availability checks of the optional libraries (a port of coola.utils.imports), MissingPackageError, lazy_exports. none utils Registry[T], run_command, fetch_data/fetch_response, PackageSpec, the platform of the interpreter. command.py (subprocess), http.py (network) version Version comparison and filtering, the version request, pyproject bounds, PyPI metadata (fetch_pypi_project). pypi.py, package.py (network) compat Target, the registry, the shipped data, the discovery from PyPI, the wheel tags. discover.py (network), shipped.py (read files) install The installers, the dependency resolvers, install_package and friends. installer.py (subprocess) cli The click commands; they only parse and print. none of its own

feu.github and feu.local_git are outside the chain and only use the lower layers.

docs.title: Data flow
docs.text:
1. dev/generate_compat_data.py calls discover_compat_targets(package). It fetches the project once with the Simple API (fetch_pypi_project), parses the wheel file names (parse_wheel_filename) and writes feu/compat/data/<package>.json.
  2. get_default_compat_registry() lists the files with importlib.resources (nothing is parsed). The first lookup of a package parses its file.
  3. find_closest_version(package, request, target) resolves the version request against the known versions and the ranges of the target. install_package_closest_version calls it with the full current target.
  4. The Installer resolves the dependencies with the resolver registry and runs one command: <sys.executable> -m pip install ... or uv pip install --python <sys.executable> ....

docs.title: How to add a package
docs.text:
Run the generator with the name of the package. The list of packages is the list of files, so nothing else is edited:

python dev/generate_compat_data.py --new my-package

The bot workflow bot-update-discovered-compat refreshes every file each week.

docs.title: How to add a companion or an ignored version
docs.text:
Some packages publish their platform wheels in another package. COMPANIONS in feu/compat/discover.py describes them with data:

>>> from feu.compat import COMPANIONS
>>> COMPANIONS["jax"]
SameVersion(package='jaxlib')
>>> COMPANIONS["pydantic"]
PinnedDependency(package='pydantic-core')

SameVersion means that the companion has a release with the same version, PinnedDependency that the release pins the companion release. For such a package a pure-Python wheel never counts: the release is judged by its platform wheels, or by the wheels of the companion release. A one-off case does not need an edit of the table, pass companion= or ignore_versions= to discover_compat_targets.

docs.title: How to add an installer
docs.text:
An installer is a subclass of Installer that only differs by its prefix. Register the class under a name:

>>> from feu.install import Installer, get_default_installer_registry, register_installer
>>> class PdmInstaller(Installer):
...     prefix = ("pdm", "add")
>>> register_installer("pdm", PdmInstaller)
>>> get_default_installer_registry().find("pdm") is PdmInstaller
True
>>> from packaging.requirements import Requirement
>>> PdmInstaller("--dev").command([Requirement("numpy==2.0.2")])
['pdm', 'add', '--dev', 'numpy==2.0.2']

Override check_available() to raise a RuntimeError when the tool is missing. Every function that installs takes an optional registry= if you do not want to change the default registry.

docs.title: How to add a resolver
docs.text:
A resolver is a function from a PackageSpec to a list of requirements. It receives a version request and should reason on the whole request (pandas==2.* straddles the threshold of numpy<2.0.0, "" is the latest version):

>>> from packaging.requirements import Requirement
>>> from feu.install import register_resolver
>>> from feu.install.resolver import default_resolver, resolve
>>> from feu.utils.package import PackageSpec
>>> def my_resolver(package):
...     return [*default_resolver(package), Requirement("typing-extensions>=4")]
>>> register_resolver("my-package", my_resolver)
>>> resolve(PackageSpec("My_Package", "1.0"))
[<Requirement('My_Package==1.0')>, <Requirement('typing-extensions>=4')>]

For a package that needs numpy<2.0.0 below a version, add the version to NUMPY2_MIN_VERSION in feu/install/resolver.py or use numpy2_resolver(min_version).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Unit tests mirror the source tree and are fast: no network, no real installer. Every patched behaviour has an integration test in tests/integration/ that exercises the real thing, for example tests/integration/install/test_pip_offline.py builds a wheel and runs the real pip and uv with --dry-run --no-index --find-links. The shipped data is asked real questions in tests/integration/compat/test_data.py and its contract is checked by tests/unit/compat/test_shipped_data.py.

docs.title: feu.compat
docs.text: Registry-based package/Python-version compatibility resolution: given a package name and a target environment, find out which versions of that package are known to work.

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
• Target identifies the environment a constraint applies to: python_version and free_threaded (always concrete), plus optional os/arch. None on os/arch means "any" when stored in the registry, and "unspecified" when used as a lookup key.
  • VersionRange is one contiguous (min, max) span of valid package versions; either bound may be None for unbounded. A package/target can have several disjoint ranges (e.g. a package supported 1.0-1.10, then unsupported for a stretch, then supported again from 2.8 onward).
  • CompatRegistry stores package constraints populated from the shipped data of feu/compat/data (one JSON file per package, parsed the first time the package is looked up, see get_default_compat_registry()), and user calls to register_compat(). A target registered with an empty list of ranges is explicitly unsupported, whereas a package/target with no entry is unconfigured and accepts any version.

A lookup target matches a stored entry when python_version and free_threaded are equal, and each of os/arch is None in the entry (wildcard), None in the lookup (unspecified: any platform) or equal. Among the matching entries, the most specific ones (most non-None os/arch) are kept and the answer is the union of their ranges.

docs.title: Discovery
docs.text:
discover_compat_targets(pkg_name, targets=DEFAULT_TARGETS, *, companion=None, ignore_versions=None) computes compatibility data from PyPI rather than requiring it to be hand-maintained, with one algorithm for every package. For each release, it parses the wheel file names (via WheelTag / parse_wheel_filename) and the requires-python metadata to determine, per target (Python version, OS, arch, free-threaded), the range of package versions that support it. It returns a Discovery: the considered versions and the ranges of each target.

A package whose wheels do not carry the platform tags is described by data, not by a class: a companion package (SameVersion("jaxlib") for jax, PinnedDependency("polars-runtime-32") for polars, PinnedDependency("pydantic-core") for pydantic, see COMPANIONS) and the releases to ignore (IGNORED_VERSIONS, e.g. duckdb 0.0.0). For such a package a pure-Python wheel says nothing about the platform and never counts: the release is judged by its platform wheels, or by the wheels of the companion release. Pass companion= or ignore_versions= to handle a new case.

The discovered data is the built-in compatibility data: one JSON file per package in feu/compat/data/<canonical-name>.json (the format is documented in feu.compat.shipped), regenerated by dev/generate_compat_data.py and run on a schedule by the bot-update-discovered-compat CI workflow (.github/workflows/bot-update-discovered-compat.yaml). The list of packages is the list of files: add a package with python dev/generate_compat_data.py --new <package>, no other file is edited. CompatRegistry.packages() lists them without parsing any file.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
>>> from feu.compat import Target, find_closest_version, is_valid_version
>>> target = Target(python_version="3.11")
>>> is_valid_version("numpy", "1.23.2", target)
True
>>> find_closest_version("numpy", "0.1.0", target)
'...'

Corrections can be registered on top of the built-in data:

>>> from feu.compat import Target, register_compat
>>> from feu.compat.registry import VersionRange
>>> register_compat({"mypkg": {Target(python_version="3.12"): [VersionRange("2.0", None)]}})

docs.title: feu.compat
docs.text: Contain a registry-based system for package/target compatibility resolution.

docs.title: feu.compat.CompatRegistry
docs.text:
Manage package version compatibility across different compatibility targets.

The registry maps the canonical package name (PEP 503) to Target to a list of VersionRange. A package version is valid for a target if it falls within any of the registered ranges; an empty list means no version is valid for that target. A lookup target matches a stored entry when python_version and free_threaded are equal, and each of os/arch is None in the stored entry (wildcard), None in the lookup target (unspecified, i.e. any platform) or equal. Among all matching entries, the most specific ones (most non-None os/arch fields) are kept and the answer is the union of their ranges. A lookup target that leaves os/arch to None therefore gets the versions published for at least one platform.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[str, dict[Target, list[VersionRange]]] | None

Optional initial mapping of package constraints. If provided, the state is deep-copied to prevent external mutations. It is validated like register, and the package names are canonicalised.

None loader DataLoader | None

Optional loader of the data of the packages. The data of a package is loaded the first time the package is looked up or registered into, so creating the registry and listing its packages cost nothing. A registration into a package that is not loaded yet loads it first, so the conflict check and exist_ok see the loaded entries.

None version_source Callable[[str], Iterable[str]] | None

Optional function that returns the releases of a package (given its canonical name), in any order. It is called only to match a wildcard request (e.g. "2.*") or to list versions, never for an exact version or for the latest version, and only for a package that has ranges. The versions registered with register_versions take precedence. Without a source, a wildcard can only be matched against registered versions. An error of the source (e.g. no network) is not caught.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a range of initial_state is invalid (see register).

Example 
>>> from feu.compat import CompatRegistry, Target
>>> from feu.compat.registry import VersionRange
>>> registry = CompatRegistry()
>>> registry.register(
...     pkg_name="numpy",
...     target=Target(python_version="3.11"),
...     ranges=[VersionRange("1.23.2", "2.4.6")],
... )
>>> registry.is_valid_version("numpy", "2.0.2", Target(python_version="3.11"))
True

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default pkg_name str

The package name to check (e.g., "numpy").

required

str

str

docs.text:
Define the compatibility registry for package version resolution.

This module provides a registry system that manages and resolves valid package version ranges per compatibility target, enabling lookup of the closest valid version and validation of a given version.

docs.title: feu.compat.registry.CompatRegistry
docs.text:
Manage package version compatibility across different compatibility targets.

The registry maps the canonical package name (PEP 503) to Target to a list of VersionRange. A package version is valid for a target if it falls within any of the registered ranges; an empty list means no version is valid for that target. A lookup target matches a stored entry when python_version and free_threaded are equal, and each of os/arch is None in the stored entry (wildcard), None in the lookup target (unspecified, i.e. any platform) or equal. Among all matching entries, the most specific ones (most non-None os/arch fields) are kept and the answer is the union of their ranges. A lookup target that leaves os/arch to None therefore gets the versions published for at least one platform.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default initial_state dict[str, dict[Target, list[VersionRange]]] | None

Optional initial mapping of package constraints. If provided, the state is deep-copied to prevent external mutations. It is validated like register, and the package names are canonicalised.

None loader DataLoader | None

Optional loader of the data of the packages. The data of a package is loaded the first time the package is looked up or registered into, so creating the registry and listing its packages cost nothing. A registration into a package that is not loaded yet loads it first, so the conflict check and exist_ok see the loaded entries.

None version_source Callable[[str], Iterable[str]] | None

Optional function that returns the releases of a package (given its canonical name), in any order. It is called only to match a wildcard request (e.g. "2.*") or to list versions, never for an exact version or for the latest version, and only for a package that has ranges. The versions registered with register_versions take precedence. Without a source, a wildcard can only be matched against registered versions. An error of the source (e.g. no network) is not caught.

None

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

If a range of initial_state is invalid (see register).

Example 
>>> from feu.compat import CompatRegistry, Target
>>> from feu.compat.registry import VersionRange
>>> registry = CompatRegistry()
>>> registry.register(
...     pkg_name="numpy",
...     target=Target(python_version="3.11"),
...     ranges=[VersionRange("1.23.2", "2.4.6")],
... )
>>> registry.is_valid_version("numpy", "2.0.2", Target(python_version="3.11"))
True

docs.title: feu.compat.shipped
docs.text:
Contain the loader of the shipped compatibility data.

The data is one JSON file per package in feu/compat/data/, named by the canonical package name (PEP 503):

.. code-block:: json

{
  "package": "numpy",
  "generated": "2026-11-09",
  "targets": [
    {"python": "3.12", "free_threaded": false, "os": "linux", "arch": "x86_64",
     "ranges": [["1.26.0", null]]}
  ]
}

There is no list of versions: a wildcard request is matched against the releases downloaded from PyPI (see CompatRegistry), so it never goes stale. A range whose max is null is open: the latest release was compatible when the file was generated. The entries are sorted by (python, free_threaded, os, arch).

The list of packages is the list of files, so a package is added by running dev/generate_compat_data.py with its name.

docs.text:
Contain the parser of the tags of a wheel file name.

The file name is parsed by packaging.utils.parse_wheel_filename, which expands the compressed tag sets (e.g. macosx_10_9_x86_64.macosx_11_0_arm64). Each (interpreter, abi, platform) is then mapped to a WheelTag.

The platforms that feu knows are linux, macos and windows on x86_64 and arm64 (the vocabulary of Target). The other platforms (musllinux, win32, i686, armv7l, ppc64le, ...) and the other interpreters (PyPy, GraalPy, ...) are out of scope: they give no tag.

install_package_closest_version(
    installer: InstallerSpec,
    package: PackageSpec,
    *,
    target: Target | None = None,
    registry: Registry[type[Installer]] | None = None,
) -> None

Install a package and associated packages by using the specified installer.

This function finds the closest valid version if the specified version is not compatible with the target. By default, the target is the current environment: the Python version, the free-threaded flag, the OS and the CPU architecture.

The package version is a version request: an exact version ('2.0.2'), a wildcard ('2.*') or '' for the latest version. A request is resolved to the latest compatible version. If that version lies in an open-ended range, the request itself is installed, so the installer picks the real latest release.

required package PackageSpec

required target Target | None

The installer registry. None means the default registry.

None

Type Description RuntimeError

If no installer is registered for the installer name, or if the tool of the installer is not available.

UnsupportedVersionError

If no version of the package is valid for the target, or if no known version satisfies a wildcard request.

ValueError

If the package version is not a valid version request.

CalledProcessError

If the installation command fails.

>>> from feu.install import InstallerSpec, install_package_closest_version

>>> install_package_closest_version(

This function performs an HTTP GET request and parses the response body as JSON.     *,
    timeout: float = 10.0,
    headers: Mapping[str, str] | None = None,
    params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None,
    accept: str | None = None,
) -> Response

Retrieve data from a given URL with automatic retry logic.

This function performs an HTTP GET request with a configured retry policy for transient errors (429, 500, 502, 503, 504), with exponential backoff and up to 5 retry attempts on https:// and http://.     path: str | Path, *, package: str | None = None

Read a pyproject.toml file and return the version bounds of its dependencies.

The file is parsed once. The following standard sections are read, in this order:

  • [project.optional-dependencies.*]

required package str | None

None

Raises:

Type Description FileNotFoundError

If the file does not exist.

TOMLDecodeError

If the file is not valid TOML.

Example 
bounds = read_pyproject_bounds("pyproject.toml", package="numpy")
for b in bounds:
    print(b.section, b.lower, b.upper)

  • [project.optional-dependencies.*]
  • [dependency-groups.*] (the {include-group = ...} entries of PEP 735 are skipped)

The names of the returned bounds are canonical (PEP 503).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str | Path

Path to the pyproject.toml file.

required package str | None

If specified, only the occurrences of this package are returned. The comparison uses the canonical names, so it is case-insensitive and treats hyphens, underscores and dots as equivalent.

None

Returns:

Type Description list[PackageBounds]

A list of PackageBounds instances, one per occurrence in the sections above. The section field gives the section, e.g. 'project.optional-dependencies.dev'.

Raises:

Type Description FileNotFoundError

If the file does not exist.

TOMLDecodeError

If the file is not valid TOML.

Example 
bounds = read_pyproject_bounds("pyproject.toml", package="numpy")
for b in bounds:
    print(b.section, b.lower, b.upper)
